title: The sign of the endless light
hook: a pillar of light with no end, a flower that lied, and why Shiva is worshipped as a smooth stone
carry: the lingam is a sign of the endless light

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poison from the churned ocean, the blue throat, and milk poured until dawn. Your line was shiva drank the poison; we keep him company.

Brahma and Vishnu are arguing over who matters more when a column of fire bursts up between them, with no top and no bottom. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Neither finds an end, and Vishnu comes back and says so. You heard that on day ninety. Tonight, look again at two things. A small, sweet-smelling flower, drifting down out of the dark. And the pillar itself, which didn't stay in the story. You'll find it at the center of almost every Shiva temple.
screen: `A PILLAR WITH NO END.` → `A FLOWER DRIFTING DOWN.` → `IN EVERY SHIVA TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the flower has a name: ketaki, the fragrant screwpine blossom. Brahma, worn out and empty-handed, meets it falling from far above, and asks a favor. Back me up. The flower agrees. Brahma claims he reached the top, and the ketaki says yes, I saw him there. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out. Vishnu, who admitted his limit, is honored. Brahma is rebuked, and the flower gets its own sentence: never to be offered in Shiva's worship. Now the pillar. Walk into a Shiva temple and at the center you usually won't find a statue with a face. You'll find a smooth, rounded stone on a base: the lingam. Linga means sign, or mark. Hindus understand it as a sign of that pillar: Shiva as light with no top and no bottom, the God no single shape can hold. That's the teaching. The lingam isn't a portrait of Shiva. It points to what can't be pictured. Hindus also speak of twelve jyotirlingas, jyotis meaning light, shrines where Shiva is said to have shown himself as that light: Somnath on the Gujarat coast, Kashi Vishwanath in Varanasi, Kedarnath in the Himalayas, Rameshwaram in the far south, and eight more. This is a Shaiva story, told by Shiva's devotees; Vaishnava Hindus tell stories where Vishnu is the source, and Hindus hold these side by side. And today: when a friend asks why Hindus pray to a stone, you have the answer. It's not the stone. It's what the stone points to.
screen: `THE KETAKI SAYS YES.` · `THE FALSE WITNESS IS BARRED.` · `LINGA: A SIGN.` · `JYOTIRLINGA: TWELVE SHRINES OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `IT POINTS TO WHAT CAN'T BE PICTURED.`

segments.voice: Picture a smooth dark stone in front of you, with water running down it. Now let it stretch upward, past the ceiling, and downward, past the floor, with no end either way, just light. You can't see the top. You don't need to. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya once. Then let the picture settle back into a small stone, and notice that it still points to all of that.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, which many say remembers the pillar of light that had no end.
Your line: the lingam is a sign of the endless light. Not the stone; what it points to. Day one hundred forty-nine, done.

screen: `DAY 149 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES THE RAKHI PRAYER NAME A KING?`

howItsDone: Many Hindus remember the Lingodbhava, Shiva appearing from an endless pillar of light, on Maha Shivaratri; they worship Shiva in the lingam, a sign of that light, temples often show the scene carved on the back wall of the shrine, and the twelve jyotirlinga temples draw crowds through the night.
